409.t: Excelsior Brass Band and teacher Charlie Lipscomb
409.s: He remembers no country blues singers, only the Excelsior Brass Band in which his teacher Charlie Lipscomb played, the man who forbade jazz.
409.q: No. The only bands I remember was the brass band, the Excelsior Brass Band, which my teacher was

409.s: His teacher hit him if he got nervous, and Cootie says he was never nervous in his career.
409.ch: First bands and the road in the South
409.q: By -- if I'd get nervous like that, he'd hit me and say, 'Don't you ever get nervous doing nothing in music. Because you can't produce when you get nervous.' And he'd hit me like that. 'Don't you never.'

31.t: New England Conservatory, a Russian-trained teacher and early Boston piano jobs
31.s: Whaley left the Conservatory, studied with a strict teacher, graduated in 1911, then played cabarets in Boston, learned to transpose for song pluggers and prided himself on sight reading.
31.ch: Early life and training in Boston
31.q: : The only thing I know about the south was when I traveled in it. See, I did a lot -- after I got in high school, see, I went to New England Conservatory for about six months and they didn't pay me no mind, see, so I quit there and I got a teacher, he perfected (at) the Russian Conservatory and he…

31.s: He returns to the Conservatory and his Sunday $10 lessons with a Russia-trained teacher whose family listened in.
31.ch: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
31.q: Sure, Boston was a music culture place there. You know, I was -- I went to the conservatory, see, for about six months, but see, they didn't give me the attention, and a guy says, 'Hey, there's a teacher who has just come back from Russia, he had perfected at the Conservatory of Russia' -- and I…

174.t: Lessons with Professor Nickerson and his daughter Camille
174.s: Dejan started lessons around age nine or ten with Professor Nickerson, a violinist who taught all instruments; he recalls Camille Nickerson and Creole songs, and quit after about a year over outside music.
174.q: Well, Professor Nickerson was a great violin player. Very wonderful violin player, but he taught all instruments. His daughter, Camille Nickerson, was a very fine pianist. She's in Howard University now, in Washington, I think. Well, I'd like to meet her. I'd like to meet her. She should remember,…

929.t: Classical training of the New Orleans men and the Arban book
929.s: He says New Orleans players often had real classical training, citing Kid Thomas and Manuel Perez's markings in the Arban book; Allen asks if all should learn piano.
929.q: Yeah, well, I'll just finish it up briefly on chords. These are just, it kind of starts at the beginning. These are the basic things you have before you start thinking about style or anything else. And it would be wonderful for all the musicians to have a complete training in classical music. Real,…

781.t: Learning music through the Louisiana Freedmen Baptist Association
781.s: He began learning music in school through a Baptist association in 1909.
781.q: I got started on music in school. See, I was under man, post-man started, I was going to school, I was going to school, and I was going to print and take music through an association, which was called the Louisiana Friedman, the Baptist Association, you know, of all the people. Louisiana what?…

298.t: Early lessons near the Humphrey family
298.s: Took lessons twice a week after school from the old man Humphrey, near Liberty and Cadiz.
298.q: The old man. Yeah, the old man. The Willie Graham. The old man. Yeah. The old man. Yeah. They lived on Clow or Willow Street, between Janet and Cadiz. They used to go there and take my lessons. I was going to school then, but I was going to take my lessons. Where I went. Up around Cadiz and Liberty…

59.t: Classical study with his uncle Anton Rovinsky
59.s: Hyman studied with several teachers and finally with his uncle, concert pianist Anton Rovinsky.
59.q: Yeah. I studied with an uncle of mine, other teachers too, but finally I was proficient enough to study with an uncle of mine who was a concert pianist. His names was Anton Rovinsky. And I learned a lot of things from him. I’m still learning from him actually, in a sense.

410.t: Studying with Sanford Gold, paid for by Ruby Braff
410.s: Ruby Braff urges lessons with Sanford Gold; Braff and Bradley offer to pay, and Gold's gift for hearing fingerings.
410.q: About 15 or so. Yeah. And one last thing that was probably a real key component of all these things in terms of getting into school and becoming more professional was that at the Jazz Museum one of Jack Bradley’s closest friends was the cornetist Ruby Braff. And Ruby was a real character and I…

164.t: Lessons with Royal Brown and the goal of studio work
164.s: Lessons from age eight with city organist Royal Brown, technical work plus pop books; even at 14 he wanted to be a studio player.
164.q: Not Paderewski, but — so they thought well maybe he’s got a little talent. And between the two of them I should have. And they gave me lessons starting at eight. I took lessons from the time I was eight until sixteen, and at sixteen I just kind of went on my own from there on. And the teacher I owe…

222.t: Classical lessons and jazz teacher Wilbert Barranco
222.s: He started piano at seven or eight, tired of classical, and took an eight-month jazz crash course learning chord symbols.
222.ch: Growing up in the Bay Area
222.q: Yes. I started when I was about seven or eight. And I played — almost was a prodigy actually. That’s how they were billing me. But I finally became disinterested in classical music. I didn’t put it down, but I really wanted to play jazz, really. So I finally stopped playing. I didn’t actually stop…

153.t: Lessons with his father, then Roy Knapp in Chicago
153.s: He studied snare drum with his father for a year, then with Roy Knapp in Chicago, who moved him to mallets, harmony and theory. By 13 he was teaching in his father's store.
153.q: I studied with my father first. I did about a year with him. Then he said, “I can’t teach you anything more.” So I went to Chicago to study with Roy Knapp. Remember Roy Knapp? He taught Gene Krupa. Buddy [Rich] took a few lessons with him too. When I went to study with Roy, he had me play something…

328.t: Mr. Franzman, Mr. Brown and his genius brother's sight-reading
328.s: Two local teachers helped young musicians; Franzman taught chords in one class.
328.ch: Practice, Indianapolis memories and the trombone
328.q: We didn’t have any of that. We did have some –what we did have was the possibility of scores, some scores. And there were two men. One was named Mr. Franzman. The other was Mr. Brown. They were always helping the young musicians, encouraging them, telling them things that would be criticisms, but…

565.t: Piano lessons with Boca Negra and Margaret Barnes
565.s: Charlie recommended his teachers; Margaret Barnes taught him in the Carnegie Hall building and he gave a recital at Weill.
565.q: Always. I had the best teachers. My brother would recommend me. The first one was called Boca Negra, “black mouth” (that’s the translation). Boca Negra in the Bronx. That’s how I started. Then I went to different teachers. But my best and most important teacher was the first

509.t: Teachers Mr. Murphy and Dr. Hughes, and learning before she could read
509.s: Mr. Murphy taught her classical pieces by ear until Dr. Francis Hughes took over at eleven.
509.q: I had Mr. Murphy, who was a wonderful gentleman who just, you know, he saw something in me, and he was there until I was eleven years old. And he told Dr. Francis Hughes that, ―I‘ve taught her all I can.‖ And then she took over. Oh, I wish you‘d talk with her. She just opened things. She opened…

528.s: He started lessons at about thirteen, working on Bach, Beethoven and Hanon scales with a teacher who wanted him reading well by sixteen.
528.q: We had Bach and Beethoven book, so I mean . . . I learned how to read that music and that’s basically what-we had a book of scales, that was very prominent, a lot of piano players tried it out, Hanon, you know books like that and it was good, he was very good. He wanted to see me at sixteen being…

229.t: W.L. Jackson, his Chicago trumpet teacher
229.s: Blakeney describes teacher W.L. Jackson, a talker and violinist who raised Erskine and Charles Tate and told him to join the union.
229.q: W.L. Jackson was a great talker. He used to claim to be one of the best violinists in the country, and after I had my lesson every night he would sit down and just talk about his experiences.

614.t: Parochial school bands and private teachers Buech, Kruger and Rudy Wiedoeft
614.s: His school had little music program, so he studied privately with Arthur Buech, Arthur Kruger and Walker, plus a couple of lessons with Rudy Wiedoeft.
614.q: No, not the school I attended. Where I spent most of my years was at St. John's Cathedral Grade School and then later high school, and there was not -- they had a semblance of a band program, but not very much. But I was called upon to play constantly while I was a member of that grouping in school.

677.t: Formal teachers in the school systems
677.s: Most of his instruction was in school; he names Alfred Nord, Miss Nepert and Mr. Parker, whose wife played cello and accompanied his solos.
677.q: Yeah, it was -- most of it was in school until I got into Los Angeles where I was more or less in the professional life. Of course in Pasadena we had some pretty good instructors. In those days there were very, very good instructors in the school system.

9.t: Oboe lessons with Trogliano and long practice hours
9.s: His paid oboe teacher kept him on the C scale for six months, so he quit lessons and practiced four or five hours a day in the attic.
9.ch: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
9.q: Yeah, I went to a teacher. He used to work in the State Theatre Orchestra. His name was Trogliano(?). He was a very good oboe player himself. I didn't think much of his teaching, because he didn't teach me much. He taught me very little. In fact, he had me on the C scale for six months, and I…

452.t: No teachers in Houston: Abner Jones and the silent-movie trio
452.s: Cobb calls himself self-made; the only man who could teach theory, Abner Jones, played in a silent-movie theatre trio and had no time to teach.
452.q: All right. Abner Jones was his name, and we had a theatre here, this was during the silent movie days; it was a trio that played for the silent movies, and he was the drummer, and the xylophone player -- I didn't say vibraphone -- I said xylophone.

93.t: Tiger Flowers asks Green to teach him to tap
93.s: Flowers asks Green rather than his joker cousin to teach him tap and offers to teach him back.
93.q: So then one day, one afternoon there, here come Tiger Flowers walking across the street. Now, he was popular. He was the lightweight champion of the world at that time, Tiger Flowers, and he lived right just around the corner on Irving Street. And he says, he came walking right over across the…

473.t: The beginners' teacher who forbade jazz
473.s: Students practiced reading at home; the teacher rapped fingers of anyone who added jazz notes, yet the kids liked him, and older musicians resented that the band was training their replacements.
473.ch: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
473.q: Yeah, you'd have your music book. You'd go home and practice you know, and run over it, so you could get it right when you came back. But he didn't allow you to play jazz. No, he didn't like you to play jazz. Anytime he caught you playing jazz he'd crack you on your fingers, you know.
